Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)

- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)

- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace

% HEXYL(1) hexyl 0.12.0 | General Commands Manual
%
% 2022-12-05

# NAME

hexyl - a command-line hex viewer

# SYNOPSIS

**hexyl** [_OPTIONS_] [_FILE_]

# DESCRIPTION

**hexyl** is a simple hex viewer for the terminal.
It uses a colored output to distinguish different categories of bytes (NULL
bytes, printable ASCII characters, ASCII whitespace characters, other ASCII
characters and non-ASCII).

# POSITIONAL ARGUMENTS

_FILE_
:   The file to display.
    If no _FILE_ argument is given, read from STDIN.

# OPTIONS

**-n**, **\--length** _N_
:   Only read _N_ bytes from the input.
    The _N_ argument can also include a unit with a decimal prefix (kB, MB, ..)
    or binary prefix (kiB, MiB, ..), or can be specified using a hex number.

    Examples:

    :   

        Read the first 64 bytes:
        :   $ **hexyl \--length=64**

        Read the first 4 kibibytes:
        :   $ **hexyl \--length=4KiB**

        Read the first 255 bytes (specified using a hex number):
        :   $ **hexyl \--length=0xff**

**-c**, **\--bytes** _N_
:   An alias for **-n**/**\--length**.

**-l** _N_
:   Yet another alias for **-n**/**\--length**.

**-s**, **\--skip** _N_
:   Skip the first _N_ bytes of the input.
    The _N_ argument can also include a unit (see **\--length** for details).
    A negative value is valid and will seek from the end of the file.

**\--block-size** _SIZE_
:   Sets the size of the block unit to _SIZE_ (default is 512).

    Examples:

    :   

        Sets the block size to 1024 bytes:
        :   $ **hexyl \--block-size=1024 \--length=5block**

        Sets the block size to 4 kilobytes:
        :   $ **hexyl \--block-size=4kB \--length=2block**

**-v**, **\--no-squeezing**
:   Displays all input data.
    Otherwise any number of groups of output lines which would be identical to
    the preceding group of lines, are replaced with a line comprised of a
    single asterisk.

**\--color** _WHEN_
:   When to use colors.
    The auto-mode only displays colors if the output goes to an interactive
    terminal.

    Possible values:

    :   - **always** (default)
        - **auto**
        - **never**

**\--border** _STYLE_
:   Whether to draw a border with Unicode characters, ASCII characters, or none
    at all.

    Possible values:

    :   - **unicode** (default)
        - **ascii**
        - **none**

**-o**, **\--display-offset** _N_
:   Add _N_ bytes to the displayed file position.
    The _N_ argument can also include a unit (see **\--length** for details).
    A negative value is valid and calculates an offset relative to the end of
    the file.

**-h**, **\--help**
:   Prints help information.

**-V**, **\--version**
:   Prints version information.

# ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES

**hexyl** colors can be configured via environment variables. The variables used are as follows:

:   - **HEXYL_COLOR_ASCII_PRINTABLE**: Any non-whitespace printable ASCII character
    - **HEXYL_COLOR_ASCII_WHITESPACE**: Whitespace such as space or newline (only visible in middle panel with byte values)
    - **HEXYL_COLOR_ASCII_OTHER**: Any other ASCII character (< **0x80**) besides null
    - **HEXYL_COLOR_NULL**: The null byte (**0x00**)
    - **HEXYL_COLOR_NONASCII**: Any non-ASCII byte (> **0x7F**)
    - **HEXYL_COLOR_OFFSET**: The lefthand file offset

The colors can be any of the 8 standard terminal colors: **black**, **blue**, **cyan**, **green**, **magenta**, **red**,
**yellow** and **white**. The "bright" variants are also supported (e.g., **bright blue**). Additionally, you can use
the RGB hex format, **#abcdef**. For example, **HEXYL_COLOR_ASCII_PRINTABLE=blue HEXYL_COLOR_ASCII_WHITESPACE="bright green"
HEXYL_COLOR_ASCII_OTHER="#ff7f99"**.

# NOTES

Source repository:
:   <https://github.com/sharkdp/hexyl>

# EXAMPLES

Print a given file:
:   $ **hexyl small.png**

Print and view a given file in the terminal pager:
:   $ **hexyl big.png | less -r**

Print the first 256 bytes of a given special file:
:   $ **hexyl -n 256 /dev/urandom**

# AUTHORS

**hexyl** was written by David Peter <mail@david-peter.de>.

# REPORTING BUGS

Bugs can be reported on GitHub at:
:   <https://github.com/sharkdp/hexyl/issues>

# COPYRIGHT

**hexyl** is dual-licensed under:

:   - Apache License 2.0 (<https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0>)
    - MIT License (<https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT>)

# SEE ALSO

**hexdump**(1), **xxd**(1)
</output>

# POSITIONAL ARGUMENTS

_FILE_
:   The file to display.
    If no _FILE_ argument is given, read from STDIN.

# OPTIONS

**-n**, **\--length** _N_
:   Only read _N_ bytes from the input.
    The _N_ argument can also include a unit with a decimal prefix (kB, MB, ..)
    or binary prefix (kiB, MiB, ..), or can be specified using a hex number.

    Examples:

    :   

        Read the first 64 bytes:
        :   $ **hexyl \--length=64**

        Read the first 4 kibibytes:
        :   $ **hexyl \--length=4KiB**

        Read the first 255 bytes (specified using a hex number):
        :   $ **hexyl \--length=0xff**

**-c**, **\--bytes** _N_
:   An alias for **-n**/**\--length**.

**-l** _N_
:   Yet another alias for **-n**/**\--length**.

**-s**, **\--skip** _N_
:   Skip the first _N_ bytes of the input.
    The _N_ argument can also include a unit (see **\--length** for details).
    A negative value is valid and will seek from the end of the file.

**\--block-size** _SIZE_
:   Sets the size of the block unit to _SIZE_ (default is 512).

    Examples:

    :   

        Sets the block size to 1024 bytes:
        :   $ **hexyl \--block-size=1024 \--length=5block**

        Sets the block size to 4 kilobytes:
        :   $ **hexyl \--block-size=4kB \--length=2block**

**-v**, **\--no-squeezing**
:   Displays all input data.
    Otherwise any number of groups of output lines which would be identical to
    the preceding group of lines, are replaced with a line comprised of a
    single asterisk.

**\--color** _WHEN_
:   When to use colors.
    The auto-mode only displays colors if the output goes to an interactive
    terminal.

    Possible values:

    :   - **always** (default)
        - **auto**
        - **never**

**\--border** _STYLE_
:   Whether to draw a border with Unicode characters, ASCII characters, or none
    at all.

    Possible values:

    :   - **unicode** (default)
        - **ascii**
        - **none**

**-o**, **\--display-offset** _N_
:   Add _N_ bytes to the displayed file position.
    The _N_ argument can also include a unit (see **\--length** for details).
    A negative value is valid and calculates an offset relative to the end of
    the file.

**-h**, **\--help**
:   Prints help information.

**-V**, **\--version**
:   Prints version information.

# ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES

**hexyl** colors can be configured via environment variables. The variables used are as follows:

:   - **HEXYL_COLOR_ASCII_PRINTABLE**: Any non-whitespace printable ASCII character
    - **HEXYL_COLOR_ASCII_WHITESPACE**: Whitespace such as space or newline (only visible in middle panel with byte values)
    - **HEXYL_COLOR_ASCII_OTHER**: Any other ASCII character (< **0x80**) besides null
    - **HEXYL_COLOR_NULL**: The null byte (**0x00**)
    - **HEXYL_COLOR_NONASCII**: Any non-ASCII byte (> **0x7F**)
    - **HEXYL_COLOR_OFFSET**: The lefthand file offset

The colors can be any of the 8 standard terminal colors: **black**, **blue**, **cyan**, **green**, **magenta**, **red**,
**yellow** and **white**. The "bright" variants are also supported (e.g., **bright blue**). Additionally, you can use
the RGB hex format, **#abcdef**. For example, **HEXYL_COLOR_ASCII_PRINTABLE=blue HEXYL_COLOR_ASCII_WHITESPACE="bright green"
HEXYL_COLOR_ASCII_OTHER="#ff7f99"**.

Source repository:

# EXAMPLES

Print a given file:
:   $ **hexyl small.png**

Print and view a given file in the terminal pager:
:   $ **hexyl big.png | less -r**

Print the first 256 bytes of a given special file:
:   $ **hexyl -n 256 /dev/urandom**

python3 -c "import sys; sys.stdout.buffer.write(bytes(range(200, 256)))" | ./executable --color-scheme=gradient 2>&1 | cat -v | head -10

# Let me analyze the gradient colors for non-ASCII bytes
# 0x80 = 128: 255,0,0 (red)
# 0xc8 = 200: 255,217,0 (yellow-ish)
# 0xff = 255: 255,255,249 (white-ish)
# Let me compute the gradient formula

python3 << 'EOF'
# Non-ASCII gradient: 0x80 to 0xFF (128-255), total 128 values
# Observed:
# 0x80 (0): 255, 0, 0
# 0x81 (1): 255, 3, 0
# 0x87 (7): 255, 21, 0
# 0x88 (8): 255, 24, 0
# 0x8f (15): 255, 45, 0
# 0x90 (16): 255, 48, 0
# 0xc8 (72): 255, 217, 0
# 0xd4 (84): 255, 253, 0
# 0xd5 (85): 255, 255, 3
# 0xd7 (87): 255, 255, 14
# 0xff (127): 255, 255, 249

# Let's compute
for i in range(0, 128, 8):
    byte_val = 0x80 + i
    # two phases:
    # Phase 1: 0 to some value: R=255, G increases from 0 to 255, B=0
    # Phase 2: R=255, G=255, B increases from 0 to ?
    pass

# Looking at observations:
# 0 -> (255, 0, 0)
# 84 -> (255, 253, 0) = index 84
# 85 -> (255, 255, 3)
# So phase 1 is 0-84 (85 values), green goes 0 to 253 in 84 steps
# Phase 2 is 85 onwards
# 85 -> (255, 255, 3)
# 87 -> (255, 255, 14)
# 127 -> (255, 255, 249)
# Blue 0 to 255 in 42 steps? Wait 3 and 14 seem off

# Let me check the formula:
# For phase 1 (green): 3 * i
# 0: 3*0 = 0 ✓
# 1: 3*1 = 3 ✓
# 7: 3*7 = 21 ✓
# 15: 3*15 = 45 ✓
# 72: 3*72 = 216 ... but 217 was observed
# Hmm let me check again
# 0x80 = (255, 0, 0)
# 0x81 = (255, 3, 0) -> 3*1 = 3 ✓
# When does green reach 255?
# 3*i = 255 -> i = 85 -> 0x80 + 85 = 0xd5 -> 0xd5 = (255, 255, 3)
# 0xd4 = (255, 253, 0) -> 3*84 = 252 but observed 253 ???

# Maybe it's 3*(i+1)? No that gives wrong start
# Maybe round(255 * i / 84)?
# 0->0, 84->255
for i in range(0, 128):
    byte_val = 0x80 + i
    g_frac = i / 127.0
    g_val = round(g_frac * 255)

# The braille char for byte 0x01 is ⠁ (U+2801)
# The braille char for byte 0x02 is ⠈ (U+2808)
# Byte 0x01 = 0000 0001, ⠁ = U+2801 = braille 0000 0001
# Byte 0x02 = 0000 0010, ⠈ = U+2808 = braille 0001 0000?
# Wait, 0x2801 = 1000 0001 = braille with dot 1
# 0x2802 = braille with dot 2
# ...
# But the MAPPING might not be straightforward bit order

# Let me compute the mapping programmatically
# braille byte i corresponds to U+2800 + some_bit_reversal(i)?

# For byte 0x01 (binary 00000001):
# ⠁ = U+2801 = 2800 + 0001 -> braille 0001 = dot 1
# For byte 0x02 (binary 00000010):
# ⠈ = U+2808 = 2800 + 0008 -> braille 0008 = dots 4
# For byte 0x03 (binary 00000011):
# ⠉ = U+2809 = 2800 + 0009 -> braille 0009 = dots 1,4
# For byte 0x04 (binary 00000100):
# ⠂ = U+2802 = 2800 + 0002 -> braille 0002 = dot 2
# For byte 0x05 (binary 00000101):
# ⠃ = U+2803 = 2800 + 0003 -> braille 0003 = dots 1,2
# For byte 0x06 (binary 00000110):
# ⠊ = U+280A = 2800 + 000A -> braille 000A = dots 2,4
# For byte 0x07 (binary 00000111):
# ⠋ = U+280B = 2800 + 000B -> braille 000B = dots 1,2,4

# Let's see the pattern:
# byte bit -> braille bit mapping:
# bit 0 (LSB) of byte -> braille bit 0 (dot 1)
# bit 1 of byte -> braille bit 3 (dot 4)
# bit 2 of byte -> braille bit 1 (dot 2)
# bit 3 of byte -> braille bit 4 (dot 5)
# bit 4 of byte -> braille bit 2 (dot 3)
# bit 5 of byte -> braille bit 5 (dot 6)
# bit 6 of byte -> braille bit 6 (dot 7)
# bit 7 of byte -> braille bit 7 (dot 8)

# byte 0x01 = 00000001: bit 0 -> braille bit 0 -> braille 0001 = U+2801 ✓
# byte 0x02 = 00000010: bit 1 -> braille bit 3 -> braille 1000 = 0x08 = U+2808 ✓  
# byte 0x03 = 00000011: bits 0,1 -> braille bits 0,3 -> braille 1001 = 0x09 = U+2809 ✓
# byte 0x04 = 00000100: bit 2 -> braille bit 1 -> braille 0010 = 0x02 = U+2802 ✓
# byte 0x08 = 00001000: bit 3 -> braille bit 4 -> braille 10000 = 0x10 = U+2810 ✓
# byte 0x10 = 00010000: bit 4 -> braille bit 2 -> braille 00100 = 0x04 = U+2804 ✓
# byte 0x20 = 00100000: bit 5 -> braille bit 5 -> braille 100000 = 0x20 = U+2820
# But we said 0x20 = ' ' (space)?

# Non-printable and non-ASCII use braille mapping

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub enum ColorWhen {
    Always,
    Auto,
    Never,
    Force,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub enum BorderStyle {
    Unicode,
    Ascii,
    None,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub enum CharacterTable {
    Default,
    Ascii,
    Codepage1047,
    Codepage437,
    Braille,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub enum ColorScheme {
    Default,
    Gradient,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub enum Base {
    Binary,
    Octal,
    Decimal,
    Hexadecimal,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub enum Endianness {
    Big,
    Little,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub enum GroupSize {
    One = 1,
    Two = 2,
    Four = 4,
    Eight = 8,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub enum PanelsArg {
    Auto,
    Count(u32),
}

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct Args {
    pub file: Option<String>,
    pub length: Option<u64>,
    pub skip: Option<i64>,
    pub block_size: u64,
    pub no_squeezing: bool,
    pub color: ColorWhen,
    pub border: BorderStyle,
    pub plain: bool,
    pub no_characters: bool,
    pub characters: bool,
    pub character_table: CharacterTable,
    pub color_scheme: ColorScheme,
    pub no_position: bool,
    pub display_offset: i64,
    pub panels: Option<PanelsArg>,
    pub group_size: GroupSize,
    pub endianness: Endianness,
    pub base: Base,
    pub terminal_width: Option<u32>,
    pub print_color_table: bool,
    pub include: bool,
    pub completion: Option<String>,
    pub version: bool,
    pub help: bool,
    pub help_short: bool,
}

impl Default for Args {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Args {
            file: None,

fn print_squeeze_line(out: &mut impl Write, args: &Args, off_width: usize, 
                      show_pos: bool, show_chars: bool) -> Result<(), String> {
    match &args.border {
        BorderStyle::None => {
            // For border=none, the squeeze indicator is different
            let (left, right, v_sep) = (' ', ' ', ' ');
            let mut s = String::new();
            if show_pos {
                s.push_str("*");
                s.push_str(&" ".repeat(off_width - 1));
                s.push(' ');
            } else {
                s.push_str("* ");
            }
            writeln!(out, "{}", s.trim_end()).map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
        }
        BorderStyle::Ascii | BorderStyle::Unicode => {
            let (left, right, v_sep) = match &args.border {
                BorderStyle::Unicode => ('\u{2502}', '\u{2502}', '\u{2502}'),
                _ => ('|', '|', '|'),
            };
            let mut s = String::new();
            s.push(left);
            s.push('*');
            // fill with spaces
            let hex_w = panel_hex_width(bytes_per_unit(&args.base), args.group_size.clone() as usize);
            if show_pos {
                s.push_str(&" ".repeat(off_width - 1));
                s.push(v_sep);
            }
            // rest is empty
            // Actually from the observed output, the squeeze line is:
            // │*       │                         ┊                         │        ┊        │
            // So it's: │ + * + spaces + │ + spaces + ┊ + spaces + │ + spaces + ┊ + spaces + │
            // i.e., like a data line but with * in offset and spaces elsewhere
            writeln!(out, "{}", s).map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
        }
    }
    Ok(())
}

# So the green color applies to: 0x01-0x1f (all control chars) + 0x20 (space) + 0x7f (DEL)
# And cyan (36) applies to: 0x21-0x7e (printable non-space)
# And bright black (90) for null
# And yellow (33) for 0x80-0xff

# In our code, we have:
# COLOR_WHITESPACE (32): for is_whitespace bytes
# COLOR_OTHER_ASCII (32): for other control bytes
# Both use the same color anyway!

# So the color classification is just:
# 0x00 -> null (90)
# 0x21-0x7e -> printable (36)  
# 0x80-0xff -> nonascii (33)
# everything else (0x01-0x20, 0x7f) -> other (32)

print("0x0b should show '•'")

# Let me get the full CP1047 table from hexyl
python3 << 'EOF'
import subprocess

data = bytes(range(256))
result = subprocess.run(['./executable', '--color=never', '--character-table=codepage-1047', '--no-squeezing', '--panels=4'], 
                       input=data, capture_output=True)
output = result.stdout.decode()

# Extract char panel for each row
hexyl_cp1047 = {}
for line in output.split('\n'):
    if '│' in line and line.startswith('│'):
        parts = line.split('│')
        if len(parts) < 2:
            continue
        offset_str = parts[1].strip()
        if not offset_str:
            continue
        try:
            offset = int(offset_str, 16)
        except:
            continue
        
        # Collect all chars from char panels
        all_chars_raw = ''.join(parts[3:])  # all char parts
        all_chars = all_chars_raw.replace('┊', '')
        
        # Each char panel is 8 chars, but there might be multibyte chars
        # Let's just map them sequentially
        char_idx = 0
        for byte_offset in range(0, min(32, 256-offset)):
            if char_idx < len(all_chars):
                c = all_chars[char_idx]
                hexyl_cp1047[offset + byte_offset] = c
                char_idx += 1

# Print the table
print("hexyl CP1047 table:")
for b in range(256):
    if b in hexyl_cp1047:
        c = hexyl_cp1047[b]
        if c != '.':
            print(f"  0x{b:02x} = {repr(c)} U+{ord(c):04X}")
EOF

# That means: the space separator between bytes should be OUTSIDE the color escape
# OR: the trailing space of the last byte should be outside

# The COLOR changes PER BYTE

# BUT the space before "01" is AFTER the null color reset
# And the space after "07" is AFTER the whitespace color reset

#

# - 90m = null color
# - "00 " = null byte + space
# - 32m = whitespace color  
# - "01 02 03 04 05 06 07" = whitespace bytes with spaces between (no trailing space)
# - 39m = reset
# - " " = space after reset

# That's different from the reference which shows:
# "[90m00 [32m01 02 03 04 05 06 07[39m"
# The space after "00" is inside the [90m] region

# "[90m00 " - the "00" byte plus trailing space - then [32m starts the next group

# And the last byte group "[32m01 02 03 04 05 06 07" has NO trailing space before [39m]

# So the rule is:
# When building hex output with colors:
# - Each byte (except the last in a color group) gets: hex + " "
# - The last byte in a color group: hex only (no trailing space)
# - Then RESET
# - Then " " (the space that belongs to this position - starts the next group or padding)
# 
# Wait actually: the ref format seems to be:
# color + "xx xx xx xx" + reset + spaces
# where "xx xx xx xx" is the hex with spaces between bytes but NO trailing space

# So I need to fix my build_hex_part to not include trailing space in the colored region.

print("The fix: trailing space after last byte in a color group should be OUTSIDE the color")
EOF

fn build_char_part(bytes: &[u8], table: &CharacterTable, colorize: bool, 
                   colors: &Colors, scheme: &ColorScheme) -> String {
    let mut s = String::new();
    let mut last_color: Option<String> = None;
    
    for &b in bytes {
        let c = byte_to_char(b, table);
        
        if colorize {
            let col = byte_color(b, colors, scheme);
            if last_color.as_deref() != Some(&col) {
                s.push_str(&col);
                last_color = Some(col);
            }
        }
        s.push(c);
    }
    
    if colorize && last_color.is_some() {
        s.push_str(RESET);
    }
    
    s
}

fn write_c_include(out: &mut impl Write, data: &[u8]) -> io::Result<()> {
    if data.is_empty() {
        return Ok(());
    }
    
    let mut parts = Vec::new();
    for b in data {
        parts.push(format!("0x{:02x}", b));
    }
    writeln!(out, "  {}", parts.join(", "))?;
    Ok(())
}

fn print_color_table(out: &mut impl Write) {
    let _ = writeln!(out, "hexyl color reference:\n");
    let _ = write!(out, "\x1b[90m\u{22C4} NULL bytes (0x00)\n\x1b[39m");
    let _ = write!(out, "\x1b[36ma ASCII printable characters (0x20 - 0x7E)\n\x1b[39m");

    let _ = write!(out, "\x1b[32m\u{2022} ASCII control characters (except NULL and whitespace)\n\x1b[39m");
    let _ = write!(out, "\x1b[33m\u{00D7} Non-ASCII bytes (0x80 - 0xFF)\n\x1b[39m");
}

# The pattern: 
# 0x0 to 0xFFFFFFFF: 8 chars (8 hex digits)
# 0x100000000 to 0xFFFFFFFFFF: 10 chars (not 9!)
# 0x10000000000: 12 chars (not 11!)
# 
# It's always EVEN number of hex digits, minimum 8:
# max_offset <= 0xFFFFFFFF: 8 chars
# 0x100000000 <= max <= 0xFFFFFFFFFF: 10 chars (needs 9 digits, padded to 10)
# 0x10000000000 <= max <= 0xFFFFFFFFFFFF: 12 chars
# 
# Pattern: ceil(digits / 2) * 2, minimum 8
# Or: max(8, ceil(number of hex digits to next even)

for off in [0, 0x100, 0xFFFFFFFF, 0x100000000, 0xFFFFFFFFFF, 0x10000000000]:
    needed_digits = len(f"{off:x}")
    padded = max(8, needed_digits + (needed_digits % 2))
    print(f"0x{off:x}: digits={needed_digits}, padded={padded}")

# Hmm, does that work?
# 0x100000000: digits=9, padded=max(8,9+1)=10 ✓
# 0xFFFFFFFF: digits=8, padded=max(8,8+0)=8 ✓
# 0x10000000000: digits=11, padded=max(8,11+1)=12 ✓
# 0x1000000: digits=7, padded=max(8,7+1)=8 ✓
print()
print("Formula: max(8, digits + (digits % 2))")
EOF

#

# 
# So the reference is using BORDERED MODE width to determine number of panels,
# even for plain/border=none mode!
# 
# The fix: compute_panels should use the BORDERED width calculation even for plain/none border.

print("Issue: compute_panels uses border=none width for --plain mode")
print("Fix: use the BORDERED width calculation for determining panel count")
EOF
